title: About CIA Part 1
description: What CIA Part 1 looks like, who can sit it, how to read and answer its questions as an internal auditor, how to pace and prepare, how to book it, and how passing fits into becoming certified. Written in plain language by KaiSip from The IIA's published information.
disclaimer: Certified Internal Auditor® and CIA® are registered trademarks, and Global Internal Audit Standards™ is a trademark, of The IIA (The Institute of Internal Auditors, Inc.). KaiSip is an independent study aid. It is not affiliated with, sponsored, endorsed or licensed by The IIA. All notes and questions are written by KaiSip; none are actual exam questions. The IIA alone sets the exam rules and decides eligibility and certification. No study app can promise a pass, including this one.
check_before_booking: Fees, dates, languages and rules on this page were checked on the date shown. They can change, so check theiia.org before you book.

sections.title: The exam at a glance
sections.summary: CIA Part 1, Internal Audit Fundamentals, is 125 multiple-choice questions in 150 minutes, taken on a computer at a Pearson VUE test center. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
items: 125 multiple-choice questions in 150 minutes: 1.2 minutes, or 72 seconds, a question on average.
The IIA's published sample questions each have four options, A to D. KaiSip's practice questions use the same shape, with one best answer.
Part 1 is one of the three CIA exam parts. It is also the exam for The IIA's Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation.
Scores are reported on a scale from 250 to 750, and 600 or higher passes. 600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions.
Wrong answers are not penalized, so answer every question, including the ones you are unsure of.
No breaks are scheduled. You may step away, but the clock keeps running.
You sit the exam in person at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
The exam is non-disclosed: The IIA does not publish current questions and answers. Every KaiSip question is written by KaiSip, and none is a real exam question.
Part 1 rests on the Global Internal Audit Standards, published on 9 January 2024 and effective from 9 January 2025.

sections.title: What Part 1 is and who sits it
sections.summary: Part 1 tests the foundations: what internal auditing is for, ethics, governance, risk, control and fraud risk. Two credentials use it, and you can sit it before your work experience is complete.
items: Two routes use this exam. CIA candidates sit it as Part 1 of three. Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) candidates sit it as the IAP exam.
An active IAP holder who goes on to the CIA gets a waiver for Part 1 and sits Parts 2 and 3 only.

Entry to the three-part CIA route: a degree, or an active IAP designation. You may sit the exams before your internal audit experience is complete; the experience is needed to be certified, not to test.
The IIA does not prescribe an order for the three parts. KaiSip's view: Part 1 first suits most people, because the later parts build on its vocabulary.
Your seat in Part 1: an internal auditor who knows the rules and who does what. Several topics are about the board's or the chief audit executive's duties; you need to know them, not perform them.
The CIA program must be completed within 3 years of approval. The IAP program window is 2 years.

sections.title: The four sections and their weights
sections.summary: The IIA's syllabus splits Part 1 into four sections. A section's weight is its share of the exam, so it is a fair guide to where your study time goes.
items: Section A, Foundations of Internal Auditing, is the largest at 35%: more than one question in three. It covers the purpose, the mandate and charter, assurance and advisory services, independence and the Three Lines Model.
Section C, Governance, Risk Management, and Control, is 30%. Sections A and C together are 65% of the exam, so they come first in any review.

Section B, Ethics and Professionalism, is 20%: integrity, objectivity and its safeguards, competency, due professional care and confidentiality. Two of its six topics ask you to weigh facts and decide.
Section D, Fraud Risks, is the smallest at 15%, about one question in seven. It is tested from the internal auditor's seat: considering fraud risk and reporting concerns, not running investigations.
The syllabus lists 27 numbered topics: 8 in Section A, 6 in B, 8 in C and 5 in D. KaiSip's notes use matching codes, so 1A7 is Part 1, Section A, topic 7.

sections.title: What the syllabus verbs tell you
sections.summary: The syllabus gives no depth label for a topic. Each topic line starts with a verb, and that verb signals how deep its questions can go. The three groups below are KaiSip's reading.
items: Know and explain (Describe, Recognize, Identify, Explain): 15 of Part 1's 27 topics. Expect to pick out the right rule or role, often inside a short scenario.
Use it (Interpret, Apply, Demonstrate, Maintain): 8 topics, such as assurance against advisory services, due professional care and control types. Expect a situation and the question of what fits it.

Weigh and decide (Assess, Analyze, Determine, Evaluate): 4 topics, all in ethics and fraud. They are objectivity impairments, objectivity safeguards, fraud risk in an engagement, and fraud risk management with red flags.
A topic's detail lines can go deeper than its verb, so even a know-and-explain topic can bring a scenario. Learn each rule well enough to spot it in a story, not only to recite it.
Let the verb set your study depth. For a weigh-and-decide topic, practice until you can say why the closest wrong choice loses.

sections.title: Syllabus, languages and Topical Requirements
sections.summary: KaiSip teaches the current syllabus and the 2024 Standards. Two languages were still on the older syllabus when this page was checked, so confirm which one your exam date uses.
items: The current syllabus was live in English by July 2025. Older books and many free notes still teach the earlier exam and its vocabulary; KaiSip does not.

The three-part exam is offered in 15 languages: English; Arabic; Simplified and Traditional Chinese; French, German, Polish, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Turkish; Japanese, Korean, Thai and Vietnamese.
Caution for Arabic: candidates sit the older 2019 syllabus through 27 December 2026 and move to the current one on 28 December 2026.
Caution for Simplified Chinese (mainland China only): it was still on the older 2019 syllabus when checked, and it moves to the current one during the December 2026 testing window.
If either caution applies to you, confirm with The IIA which syllabus your exam date uses before you rely on this course.
Topical Requirements enter the exam on dates. Scored questions on a new one do not appear until at least 6 months after it takes effect.

Cybersecurity is testable now. The IIA's reference list gives start months for the others: Third-Party in March 2027, Organizational Behavior in June 2027 and Organizational Resilience in October 2027.

sections.title: Read each question as an internal auditor
sections.summary: A short routine for every question: find what is asked and who is acting, check the strength of the rule, then eliminate and choose. These are KaiSip's habits, built on the Standards.
steps: Read the last line first. Note what is asked for: an action, a person, a document, a rule or a reason.
Find the actor: an internal auditor, the chief audit executive, senior management, the board, or the managers who run the activity under review. The right answer changes with the actor.
Find the priority word, such as FIRST, BEST, MOST, PRIMARY or MOST LIKELY, and hold it in mind while you read the options.
Check the strength. Does the question ask what is required (a must) or what is good practice (a should)?
Rule out the options topic knowledge eliminates, often two. Then compare what is left: who owns the decision, function or person, and what comes first.
Say in one sentence why your choice beats the closest wrong choice. Then answer and move on.
items: Management owns risks, controls and actions. The internal auditor assesses, concludes, recommends or agrees actions, and confirms them later. An option where the auditor implements, decides or owns the fix is usually a trap.

The board approves three things for the internal audit function: its charter, its plan and its budget. Senior management gives input and support. An option with senior management approving is a rule from older books.

Independence is about where the function sits; objectivity is about one auditor's mindset. Match the fix to the problem: the board for the function's position, disclosure to the chief audit executive for a person.
Order matters: understand and plan before testing, discuss before escalating, disclose before choosing a safeguard. With FIRST, a good later step loses to the step it depends on.
Not the IT specialist, not the external auditor, not the manager. Configuring a system, giving an opinion on the financial statements and fixing the problem are other people's jobs in a CIA question.
PRIMARY asks for the main purpose, MOST LIKELY for probability and not severity, and LEAST flips the test. The full list of priority words is on the final review week's cheat sheet.

sections.title: Common traps by section
sections.summary: Each section has a few traps that catch prepared candidates. Most swap the internal auditor's seat for someone else's, or mix up a must and a should. These are KaiSip's patterns, organized by The IIA's sections.
items: Foundations: senior management approving the charter, the plan or the budget, alone or with the board. The board approves; senior management is consulted.

Foundations: treating an administrative line to the chief executive officer as a requirement. It is a leading practice. What the chief audit executive must do is confirm independence to the board at least yearly.
Foundations: calling advisory work informal. The Standards still apply, the scope is agreed with the requesting party, and management makes every decision.
Ethics: handling an objectivity problem quietly by being extra careful. The impairment is disclosed first, and the chief audit executive decides the safeguard.
Ethics: reading the 12-month line as a general ban. It is a presumption for assurance work; advisory work on a former responsibility is allowed after disclosure to the requesting party.
Governance, risk and control: the internal auditor choosing the risk response or setting risk appetite. Management chooses the response, and internal audit measures against appetite and tolerance.
Governance, risk and control: calling a frequent review or reconciliation preventive. It finds a problem after the event, so it is detective however often it runs.
Governance, risk and control: promising absolute assurance. Controls and internal audit work give reasonable assurance; judgment, error, override and collusion limit every system.
Fraud risks: considering fraud only when management asks or after a tip. It is part of every engagement risk assessment, during planning.

Fraud risks: investigating alone or confronting a suspect. On CIA questions the internal auditor usually reports through the set channel, and people with the mandate and the skills take it from there.

sections.title: Pacing your 150 minutes
sections.summary: 150 minutes for 125 questions is 1.2 minutes each. Use that number to set two checkpoints, not to time every question.
items: Checkpoints: reach question 50 by minute 60; reach question 100 by minute 120. Look at the clock at those two points and otherwise leave it alone.
Ahead at a checkpoint? The minutes you have saved are your review time. Behind? Decide a little faster on the next few questions instead of rushing all of them.
If a question stalls you, choose your best answer and move on. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess beats a blank.
No breaks are scheduled, and the clock keeps running if you take one. Plan as if you will sit straight through.
Short questions take less than the average and scenarios take more. Judge your pace at the checkpoints, never on one question.

sections.title: Your score and KaiSip's numbers
sections.summary: The IIA reports a scaled score. KaiSip never shows one: it shows the percent you got right, by section, and its own readiness band. The two are different things.
items: The IIA converts your raw score to a reporting scale that runs from 250 to 750. A scaled score of 600 or higher passes.
600 is a point on that scale, not a percent of the questions. KaiSip knows of no published way to turn a percent correct into a scaled score, and it does not try.
If you pass, your score report shows no number at all. If you do not, it shows your score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
A KaiSip mock result shows your percent correct for each section and your pace against the checkpoints. It is labeled as KaiSip's, and it is not The IIA's score.
KaiSip's readiness band is its own summary of your practice. It is a study signal, not a prediction of your result.
A good use of a practice percent: compare your four sections with each other and with last week, and give time to the section furthest behind its weight.

sections.title: Your last week before the exam
sections.summary: A calm seven-day plan with nothing new in it: one full timed mock early, then your slips, the section sheets and the close pairs, and rest at the end.
steps: Seven days out: sit one full timed mock of 125 questions in 150 minutes, using the two checkpoints. This is your last full mock before the exam.
Six days out: review each miss and name the thinking slip behind it. Then recall Sections A and C from memory and check the sheets. Stop at about 90 minutes.
Five days out: the three close pairs (must or should, function or person, approve or consult), then Section B and a short untimed set in your weakest section.
Four days out: one short timed mock. Then recall how risk drives the plan, the scope and the testing.
Three days out: Section D from the internal auditor's seat, then the principles on speaking up and on reading the question. No timed tests from today on.
Two days out: light review. Say the priority words and the answering routine from memory, then check. Confirm your appointment, ID and route.
One day out: rest. Glance at your own short list of rules, get ready for the morning, and sleep at your usual time.
items: Nothing new this week. The plan sharpens what you already know; a topic you have never studied is better left alone now.
Missed a day? Skip it and carry on with the next one. Never double up.
Recall beats rereading: answer from memory first, then check.
Practice results in any study app, including KaiSip, are not The IIA's scaled scores and cannot predict your result.

sections.title: Registering and fees
sections.summary: You apply to the CIA program, register for Part 1, then book a seat at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA's prices change on 4 January 2027.
steps: Check that you meet the entry rule for the three-part route: a degree, or an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) designation.
Apply to the CIA program and pay the application fee. Once you are approved, you have 3 years to complete the program.
Register for Part 1 and pay the exam fee. A registration lasts 180 days, unless your program expires sooner.
Book your appointment at a Pearson VUE test center inside that window.
items: Until 3 January 2027: application fee US$120 for IIA members and US$240 for non-members; Part 1 exam fee US$310 for members and US$445 for non-members.
From 4 January 2027: application fee US$145 for members and US$195 for non-members; Part 1 exam fee US$355 for members and US$475 for non-members.
These are The IIA's listed prices for the United States, Canada and some other countries. Where a national institute of The IIA runs the exams, prices may differ.
Fees are not refunded and cannot be transferred.
Need more time? On the three-part route you can buy one 75-day extension of an exam registration for US$100, and one 12-month extension of the program for US$275.
You can change an appointment up to 48 hours before it. Pearson VUE charges US$75 each time.
Sitting this exam for the Internal Audit Practitioner designation instead? That program has a 2-year window, and The IIA's IAP page gives its fees and rules.

sections.title: Test center only
sections.summary: The exam is taken in person, on a computer, at a Pearson VUE test center. The IIA ended online testing on 27 May 2025.
items: There is no at-home or online option. Advice that mentions remote testing for this exam is out of date.
Choose a test center and a time of day that suit you, and book early enough to get both. Your appointment must fall inside your 180-day registration.
You can move the appointment up to 48 hours before it, for a Pearson VUE fee of US$75 each time.
The check-in, ID and test-room rules are for The IIA and Pearson VUE to set. Read them in the current candidate handbook and in your appointment confirmation; KaiSip does not restate them.
Plan the trip ahead: know the route, the travel time and a backup, so nothing about the morning is left to chance.

sections.title: Exam day
sections.summary: Arrive with time in hand, pace by your two checkpoints, and answer every question.
items: Bring what The IIA's candidate handbook and your appointment confirmation tell you to bring. Check the ID rules a few days ahead, while there is still time to fix a problem.
125 questions in 150 minutes. Checkpoints: question 50 by minute 60; question 100 by minute 120.
No breaks are scheduled. If you take one, the clock keeps running.
Answer every question. Wrong answers are not penalized, so a best guess always beats a blank.
For each question: read the last line, find the actor and the priority word, rule out two options, then settle the final two with a principle.
If your mind goes blank, breathe out slowly, pick your best answer for now and return to it if time allows.

sections.title: After the exam
sections.summary: You do not see a score when you finish. The official result arrives within 3 weeks of your exam date.
items: No immediate unofficial score is shown. Official results arrive within 3 weeks of the exam date.
A pass report shows no numeric score. A report for an exam that was not passed shows the score and the syllabus areas that need improvement.
If you did not pass, you can sit again no sooner than 30 days after your last attempt.
An exam may be taken at most eight times during your program eligibility window, and the program's 3-year clock keeps running.
Treat a report that lists areas to improve as a study map: start with the areas it names, then compare them with your KaiSip section percents.
Passing Part 1 is one step. Parts 2 and 3, and the experience requirement, still stand between you and the CIA.

sections.title: Becoming certified
sections.summary: Passing Part 1 does not make you a Certified Internal Auditor. You also pass Parts 2 and 3 and show internal audit experience. The IIA decides every application.
steps: Pass all three parts within 3 years of your program approval. The IIA does not prescribe the order.
Show internal audit experience: 1 year with a master's degree, or 2 years with a bachelor's degree.
Or, as an active Internal Audit Practitioner (IAP) holder, show 5 years of experience. An IAP holder who also has a degree needs the 1 or 2 years that go with that degree.
items: You may sit the exams before the experience is complete. The experience is needed to be certified, not to test.
The IIA's CIA page adds that 2 of an IAP holder's 5 years must fall within the past 3 years.
The candidate handbook also lists a route with 5 years of experience and no degree, but the CIA page showed no such route when checked. If you plan to rely on it, confirm with The IIA first.
An active IAP holder has a waiver for Part 1 and sits Parts 2 and 3 only.
KaiSip has not checked the rules for keeping the certification once you hold it. Read them on The IIA's site when you get there.
